fields.hint: Picture three requests where the middle one fails. Ask what each combinator hands back in that case.
fields.explanation: Promise.allSettled waits for every input promise and always fulfills, giving one {status:"fulfilled", value} or {status:"rejected", reason} object per input, so one failure no longer discards the successes. Promise.all short-circuits: it rejects with the first rejection reason as soon as it appears, and the values that did resolve are dropped. Neither combinator changes when the work starts — both receive promises that are already running — so nothing becomes sequential, and allSettled never rejects because an input rejected.

evidence: node (22.22.2): Promise.all([60ms ok, 5ms reject, 60ms ok]) rejected at ~5ms; Promise.allSettled on the same inputs settled at ~61ms -> ["fulfilled","rejected","fulfilled"] with {status,value}/{status,reason} entries
notes: Key and all three distractors are sound; only the hint's giveaway and one spelling needed fixing.

fields.explanation: An async function always returns a promise (returning 1 gives a promise that fulfills with 1, throwing gives a rejected promise), and await simply suspends the function until a promise settles, so you can await any thenable and still attach .then/.catch to the result of an async call. Callbacks are the older pattern async/await replaced — nothing is compiled into callbacks — and no thread is involved: await moves no work off the main thread, it only lets the current function yield while the event loop keeps running. EventEmitter is a separate one-to-many notification API, not the substrate for await.

fields.hint: Ask what a deployment needs this value for: telling one running environment from another, or toggling a build flavor on and off?
fields.explanation: By convention NODE_ENV names the environment the app is running in, and the exact string "production" is what tooling checks: Express, for example, then caches compiled views and stops sending stack traces to clients, and many libraries drop development-only checks. Node itself never reads NODE_ENV — it has no built-in meaning — which is why a typo such as "Production", or leaving it unset, silently gives you development behavior on a production server. It is neither a boolean nor a build flavor, so values like "true" or "release" are just strings nothing recognizes.

fields.explanation: npm ci removes node_modules and installs the exact tree the lockfile pins. fields.hint: The name is borrowed from POSIX, but Node’s version does not duplicate the running program. Ask what it starts instead.
fields.explanation: child_process.fork(modulePath) is spawn specialized for Node: it starts a brand-new node process running the module you name — fresh memory, its own event loop, a different pid — and wires up an IPC channel so parent and child can exchange messages. Despite the name it is not POSIX fork(2): none of the parent’s memory is copied and the child begins at the first line of your module. It is not a thread either (that is worker_threads, which shares the process) and it does not go through a shell (that is exec).

fields.explanation: A forked child has its own memory, so the two sides exchange copies: the parent calls child.send(value), the child calls process.send(value), and each side receives the other’s messages through a "message" event — process.on("message") in the child, child.on("message") in the parent. Values are serialized, so functions and class instances do not survive the trip and mutating the object you sent changes nothing on the other side. Shared variables and global state cannot reach across a process boundary at all, and while argv can carry startup data it is one-way and fixed at launch.

https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/child_process.html : fork's channel "allows messages to be passed back and forth between the parent and child"
notes: Overlaps rm-node-148, which already states that fork sets up an IPC channel, but this item tests the API surface and copy semantics, so it is not a duplicate.
